title: Sinners
note: Ryan Coogler made history by simultaneously shooting on genuine 15-perf IMAX film and 5-perf Ultra Panavision 70 — the world's tallest and widest theatrical formats in a single film. DP Autumn Durald Arkapaw, the first woman to shoot a feature on 15-perf IMAX film, uses the format as emotional grammar: IMAX frames intimate and horror sequences, while Ultra Panavision governs the exterior world. Panavision built a custom Petzval lens specifically for the IMAX camera, used in a dreamlike sequence between Smoke and Annie.

title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen
note: Michael Bay followed Christopher Nolan's lead from The Dark Knight and shot three action sequences on genuine IMAX MSM 9802 cameras — the forest battle with Optimus Prime, the rail gun destroyer attack, and the Devastator pyramid assault — totaling approximately 10 minutes of native 15/70mm footage. It was only the second narrative film after The Dark Knight to use IMAX film cameras for action sequences, and the first to do so for a summer blockbuster outside of Nolan's work. The Blu-ray preserves the variable aspect ratio, with the IMAX sequences expanding to 1.43:1 and the standard footage letterboxed at 2.39:1.

title: The Dark Knight
note: Christopher Nolan shot approximately 28 minutes on 15-perf IMAX cameras — the opening bank heist, the Hong Kong skyscraper extraction, and the Batpod freeway chase. Working with DP Wally Pfister, Nolan developed lenses that could handle the enormous, loud IMAX camera in fast-moving action environments. It was the first major narrative feature to use IMAX cameras for dramatic sequences rather than nature or documentary footage.

title: The Dark Knight Rises
note: Nolan expanded dramatically — roughly 72 minutes were captured on 15-perf IMAX cameras, including the Bane aircraft heist prologue, the Gotham football stadium collapse, and most of the third-act climax. The six-minute prologue was screened exclusively in IMAX theaters before release and became a reference point for the format's potential in narrative cinema. The film shifts between IMAX's 1.43:1 ratio and 2.39:1 anamorphic, a technique Nolan has used across every subsequent production.

title: Interstellar
note: Nolan and DP Hoyte van Hoytema used IMAX cameras for all space sequences — the Gargantua black hole approach, the water planet wave, the ice planet, and the Endurance docking sequence. Van Hoytema developed specialized lens configurations to achieve the visual intimacy Nolan wanted within the mechanical constraints of a 100-lb camera. The original 15-perf 70mm print run was the largest in decades; the 2023 rerelease became one of the highest-grossing IMAX re-releases in history.

title: Dunkirk
note: Nolan and van Hoytema shot the majority of the film on IMAX cameras — including almost all aerial sequences and beach photography — a technically extreme challenge given the cameras weigh over 100 lbs and cannot be easily stabilized. To capture the Spitfire dogfights, the IMAX camera was rigged to the outside of an airworthy Spitfire using custom harnesses designed specifically for this production. No digital effects were used for the aerial sequences; every pass was a real aircraft with a real IMAX camera in formation.

title: First Man
note: Director Damien Chazelle and DP Linus Sandgren made a deliberate format decision: all Earth-bound material was shot on grainy, intimate 16mm film, while the lunar landing sequences were captured on IMAX MSM 9802 cameras in 15/70mm — the starkest possible contrast between the personal and the cosmic. The moment the film transitions to the Moon, the frame expands to the full 1.43:1 IMAX ratio, and every other visual quality changes simultaneously: grain disappears, color deepens, and the silence of space fills the expanded canvas. It was the first biographical drama to use 15/70mm IMAX cameras, applying a format previously reserved for action spectacle to a quiet moment of historical stillness.

title: Nope
note: Jordan Peele and DP Hoyte van Hoytema made Nope the first horror film — and first R-rated film — ever shot with IMAX film cameras, using the IMAX MSM 9802 for approximately 47 minutes of the final cut. Van Hoytema pushed well beyond the camera's normal static use: the massive 15-perf IMAX body was shoulder-mounted, helicopter-rigged, and deployed in configurations IMAX cameras had never been used in before. Night sequences were captured on a unique day-for-night rig pairing an infrared-modified ARRI ALEXA 65 with a Panavision System 65, with both images composited in post — the IMAX sequences expand to the native 1.43:1 ratio, revealing 40% more picture than any standard theatrical screening.

title: No Time to Die
note: The first James Bond film in the franchise's 59-year history to be shot with IMAX cameras, with DP Linus Sandgren using IMAX MKIV and MSM 9802 cameras alongside 35mm and 65mm Panavision for approximately 40 minutes of the final cut. The opening Matera chase, Norwegian river sequence, and several of the film's emotional climaxes expand to the full 1.43:1 IMAX ratio — a deliberate choice to give Bond's last chapter a larger-than-life canvas unavailable to any previous entry in the series. IMAX officially promoted it as the first Bond to carry the native aspect ratio, ending a franchise tradition of DMR-only presentations.

title: Tenet
note: Nolan and van Hoytema used both 15-perf IMAX film and IMAX-certified digital cameras, with the Oslo airport assault, Tallinn car chase, and portions of the inverted-time battle shot natively in 1.43:1. The film was notable for Nolan's insistence on a global theatrical release during COVID-19 as a statement of support for the IMAX and premium cinema ecosystem. It was the first of Nolan's productions to mix photochemical and digital IMAX capture within a single film.

title: Oppenheimer
note: For the first time in cinema history, Nolan and van Hoytema captured color images on 15-perf IMAX film — all previous 15-perf photography had been confined to action and black-and-white. The Trinity test explosion and key sequences in the "color" timeline were photographed directly on IMAX film, while the Strauss Senate hearing plays in black-and-white as a deliberate structural contrast. The film's 15-perf 70mm IMAX prints sold out weeks in advance and became the single most in-demand theatrical event of 2023.

title: Mission: Impossible Ghost Protocol
note: Brad Bird and DP Robert Elswit shot approximately 25 minutes on IMAX MSM 9802 film cameras — most memorably the Burj Khalifa glass-climbing sequence, the world's tallest building photographed at full scale on genuine 15/70mm film. Tom Cruise performed the sequence himself, hanging from the 123rd floor, with IMAX film cameras rigged to the building's exterior. The Burj sequence became a landmark demonstration of what IMAX film photography could bring to practical location action, expanding the format beyond Nolan's dark, gothic environments into pure kinetic spectacle.

title: Mission: Impossible Fallout
note: The most IMAX-intensive M:I entry, with the HALO jump (the highest free-fall ever filmed on IMAX cameras), the Paris motorcycle chase, and the Kashmir helicopter finale all shot natively for the expanded ratio. Cruise performed the 25,000-foot HALO jump himself after more than 100 practice skydives; DP Rob Hardy used natural sunrise light, giving the production zero margin for error per day. The helicopter-vs-helicopter finale in the Kashmir mountains used IMAX cameras rigged to both aircraft simultaneously.

title: Mission: Impossible Dead Reckoning Part One
note: McQuarrie and DP Fraser Taggart captured the motorcycle-off-a-cliff BASE jump — Cruise performed it after approximately 500 practice runs on a Norwegian mountainside — and the Orient Express train-roof fight with IMAX cameras. The motorbike sequence required a custom camera dolly system built into the cliff ramp to track Cruise's trajectory at IMAX scale. The train finale was shot on a working replica train set constructed on location in the UK with IMAX cameras rigged to moving carriages.

title: Mission: Impossible The Final Reckoning
note: The eighth and final installment carries the "Filmed for IMAX" designation for key action sequences, continuing the franchise's 14-year commitment to native IMAX photography. Major practical stunt sequences were captured with IMAX cameras consistent with the franchise's longstanding approach of using the format to give Cruise's physical performances their full visceral scale. Specific sequences expand to the exclusive 1.90:1 ratio in IMAX theaters.

title: Transformers: Age of Extinction
note: A landmark in IMAX history: Age of Extinction was the world premiere of IMAX's first fully-integrated digital camera — a dual 65mm 4K Vision Research Phantom 65 sensor rig — making it the first feature film ever shot with an IMAX-certified digital camera, used alongside traditional IMAX MSM 9802 film cameras for select sequences. Bay integrated both formats throughout the Hong Kong and Texas action sequences, effectively bridging the end of the IMAX film era and the beginning of certified digital IMAX. The Hong Kong Dinobots finale was designed to exploit the expanded vertical frame at maximum digital resolution.

title: Transformers: The Last Knight
note: Bay's fifth and final Transformers installment maintained IMAX capture for the Stonehenge sequence and the aerial battle finale, with DP Jonathan Sela integrating the cameras into the main photography for England-set action. The production design was scaled specifically for IMAX's taller ratio, with the medieval flashback sequences and the climactic Cybertron-Earth collision staged to fill the expanded frame.

title: Captain America: Civil War
note: The Russo Brothers and DP Trent Opaloch introduced IMAX cameras to the MCU for the Leipzig airport battle — 12 characters fighting simultaneously, with the taller ratio capturing Spider-Man's vertical web-swinging and Giant-Man's transformation at full scale. Civil War was the first MCU film to include footage shot natively for IMAX's expanded aspect ratio, beginning a practice that has continued through every subsequent MCU production. In IMAX, the airport sequence shows 26% more of the frame vertically than in standard theaters.

title: Sully
note: Clint Eastwood and DP Tom Stern shot virtually the entire film on the ARRI ALEXA 65 — the IMAX-proprietary large-format digital camera co-developed by ARRI and IMAX — making Sully the first feature film shot almost entirely on IMAX's own camera system. IMAX CEO Richard Gelfond called it "the first film where virtually the entire movie was made with IMAX technology," a milestone in the transition from IMAX film cameras to certified digital. The Hudson River water landing sequences were photographed in full 1.90:1 to give the crash and rescue the expansive visual scale the real-world event commanded.

title: Doctor Strange
note: Scott Derrickson and DP Ben Davis used IMAX cameras for the Mirror Dimension sequences and the Hong Kong time-reversal battle, where a collapsing and reversing cityscape fills the entire IMAX frame. The Dormammu sequences in the Dark Dimension were captured in IMAX to emphasize Strange's smallness against the cosmic backdrop, using the taller frame to make the scale of the threat physically overwhelming. It was the first MCU film to use IMAX cameras for otherworldly visual sequences rather than purely physical action.

title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2
note: James Gunn and DP Henry Braham shot select sequences in IMAX including the opening baby Groot battle and Ego's planetary core sequences, continuing the MCU's post-Civil War practice of deploying IMAX cameras for standout set-pieces. The Ego sequences used the full vertical IMAX frame to convey the character's literal planetary scale — his face emerging from the surface of his own world. Gunn's later productions (Suicide Squad, Guardians Vol. 3, Superman) would expand his IMAX usage dramatically.

title: Thor: Ragnarok
note: Taika Waititi and DP Javier Aguirresarobe shot the gladiatorial arena and key Asgard sequences with IMAX cameras, using the format's vertical height to capture the arena crowd surrounding Thor and Hulk from floor to ceiling. The production, filmed primarily in Australia, integrated IMAX cameras into the main photography for the film's most theatrical sequences. The vibrant Kirby-inspired color palette and theatrical staging were specifically designed to fill the expanded IMAX canvas.

title: Avengers: Infinity War
note: The Russo Brothers made Infinity War the first MCU film shot entirely with IMAX-certified cameras — DP Trent Opaloch framed every scene in the 1.90:1 ratio with 76 principal cast members across six countries and three years of production. The decision was driven by the unprecedented scope: with this many characters and this much visual information, the directors wanted audiences to see as much as possible in every frame. In IMAX, viewers see 26% more image than standard theaters at all times throughout the film.

title: Ant-Man and the Wasp
note: Peyton Reed and DP Dante Spinotti deployed IMAX cameras for the San Francisco car chase — where size-shifting vehicles cause chaos in dense traffic — and the quantum realm diving sequences. The vertical IMAX frame was particularly effective for the scale-shift comedy, capturing both giant-sized cars and the surrounding environment simultaneously without cutaways. The quantum realm sequences used IMAX's full height to create a visually overwhelming field of crystalline structures around the Wasp and Janet van Dyne.

title: Avengers: Endgame
note: The Russo Brothers and Trent Opaloch shot the entire film in IMAX, with the time heist sequences across multiple eras and the final battle — staged with over 3,000 costumed extras — composed natively for 1.90:1 throughout. The "Avengers Assemble" portal sequence and the final charge were choreographed specifically to maximize the IMAX frame's vertical dimension, with characters appearing from every level of the frame simultaneously. As the highest-grossing film of all time upon release, Endgame represented the largest IMAX theatrical event in cinema history.

title: Captain Marvel
note: Directors Boden and Fleck and DP Ben Davis used IMAX cameras for the space sequences and the binary power-unleashed third act, using the format's vertical expanse to fill the frame with Carol's energy constructs and Kree warship destruction. The binary sequence — Carol flying through an entire Kree fleet — was shot natively for IMAX to give the viewer an unobstructed sense of her scale and speed. The film was Brie Larson's introduction to the format she would return to in The Marvels.

title: Spider-Man: Far From Home
note: Jon Watts and DP Matthew Libatique used IMAX cameras for the illusion-battle sequences and Venice canal attack, with Mysterio's constructs — giant Elemental creatures and the mirror dimension fight — designed to overwhelm the IMAX frame from every direction. The Prague sequence and Tower Bridge fight were captured for IMAX's taller ratio, making Mysterio's illusions appear to surround the viewer rather than just fill a screen. The film's IMAX sequences mark the last Phase 3 Marvel production before the fully IMAX-committed Phase 4 era.

title: Black Widow
note: Cate Shortland and DP Gabriel Beristain used IMAX cameras for the opening titles sequence and the Red Room assault — a sky-platform action sequence that uses IMAX's vertical height to emphasize the characters' exposure above the clouds. The Red Room finale was staged as a vertical descent through the facility with IMAX cameras tracking action across multiple levels simultaneously. It was the first solo MCU film released after the COVID-19 pandemic gap to incorporate native IMAX photography.

title: Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings
note: Destin Daniel Cretton and DP Bill Pope used IMAX cameras for the Macao bus fight and the Ta Lo final battle, with the taller frame capturing the full choreographic scope of Simu Liu's wushu-influenced sequences across multiple vertical planes of action. The Dweller-in-Darkness and the Great Protector dragon were specifically designed to fill IMAX's expanded ratio, emphasizing mythological scale in a way standard widescreen cannot. The film was among the first MCU productions shot natively in IMAX to be designed for an Asian-led cast and setting.

title: Eternals
note: Chloé Zhao and DP Ben Davis shot the entire film in open matte with IMAX-certified cameras — meaning no portion of the image is ever masked, and IMAX theaters show the literal full frame as photographed on set. Zhao's documentary-influenced approach treated IMAX as a canvas for natural light and natural landscapes: the Babylonian, Mesopotamian, and South Dakota sequences were all captured in available light at maximum resolution. It is one of the few MCU films where the image in IMAX is exactly what Zhao saw through the viewfinder.

title: Spider-Man: No Way Home
note: Jon Watts and DP Mauro Fiore used IMAX cameras for the Statue of Liberty finale — the film's emotional and visual climax — with the scaffolding collapse and three Spider-Men fighting across vertical architecture choreographed specifically for the IMAX frame's height. The sequence was designed so that at any given moment, action is happening at the top, middle, and bottom of the IMAX frame simultaneously, requiring standard theaters to letterbox and miss content. The IMAX version shows 26% more of the final battle than any non-IMAX screening.

title: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
note: Sam Raimi and DP John Mathieson shot the entire film on IMAX-certified Panavision DXL2 cameras — the first time this large-format camera was used for a complete IMAX production. Every frame is native 1.90:1, and Raimi used the taller format to accentuate his characteristic Dutch angles, vertical horror imagery, and the physical dominance of Scarlet Witch. The Kamar-Taj siege, the Illuminati council chamber, and every multiverse incursion were staged to exploit the full IMAX height.

title: Thor: Love and Thunder
note: Taika Waititi and DP Barry Idoine shot approximately 35 minutes in IMAX's exclusive 1.90:1 ratio — specifically the Omnipotent City and the third-act shadow realm — with the remainder of the film in 2.39:1 anamorphic. The black-and-white shadow realm sequence is an unusual use of IMAX in that the format was chosen for its monochromatic impact rather than scale alone. In standard theaters, the frame letterboxes during the 2.39:1 sections and visibly expands during the IMAX sequences.

title: Black Panther: Wakanda Forever
note: Ryan Coogler and DP Autumn Durald Arkapaw — the same pair who would later shoot Sinners on 70mm IMAX film — used IMAX-certified cameras for the Wakanda vs. Talokan battles, with the expanded frame capturing the full scale of underwater armies emerging from the ocean. Coogler also deployed IMAX for emotionally heightened moments like Queen Ramonda's funeral, using the format's vertical intimacy rather than just its scale. Arkapaw was the first Black woman to serve as director of photography on an MCU film.

title: Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania
note: Peyton Reed and DP Bill Pope used IMAX cameras throughout, exploiting the taller frame to depict the physically disorienting and architecturally surreal scale of the Quantum Realm — environments with no horizon line and structures that dwarf the human characters in every direction. Kang the Conqueror was costumed and staged to fill the IMAX frame top-to-bottom in his scenes with Scott Lang, using the format to establish immediate visual dominance. The film's visual departure from previous Ant-Man productions was driven largely by this embrace of IMAX as the primary compositional frame.

title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3
note: James Gunn and DP Henry Braham shot the entire film with IMAX-certified cameras, composing every frame in 1.90:1 — the most IMAX-comprehensive Guardians production and one of the most immersive MCU IMAX experiences. The High Evolutionary's Counter-Earth and the orgosphere sequences were designed for the vertical IMAX frame to convey biological scale and surrealist excess simultaneously. The one-take corridor battle in the third act was choreographed as a continuous theatrical performance within IMAX's full canvas.

title: The Marvels
note: Director Nia DaCosta and DP Sean Bobbitt shot the entire film with IMAX-certified cameras, with each protagonist's power-swapping sequences and the space sequences designed for the taller ratio. The Aladna musical sequence — a planet where all communication is sung — used IMAX's vertical height to capture elaborate choreography from floor to ceiling. It was one of the first MCU productions directed entirely by a woman and shot wholly in IMAX.

title: Captain America: Brave New World
note: DP Kramer Morgenthau shot with Arri Alexa LF and Mini LF IMAX cameras, switching to Ultra Panatar II lenses specifically for IMAX sequences — over 30 minutes of the film expand to the exclusive 1.90:1 EAR. The action sequences were choreographed to maximize the expanded vertical frame, with Sam Wilson's aerial combat designed to use the full height of the IMAX image. The production continued the MCU's practice of integrating IMAX capture into main photography rather than treating it as a post-production addition.

title: Thunderbolts
note: DP Andrew Droz Palermo used Arri Alexa 35, Mini LF, and Red Komodo-X cameras with IMAX certification, with over 60 minutes of the film's runtime — more than half — presented in the exclusive 1.90:1 EAR. Unusually for an MCU production, the IMAX format was deployed for intimate character scenes as well as action, reflecting the film's psychologically driven tone. The opening stunt sequence was specifically designed and shot to exploit the full IMAX vertical height.

title: The Fantastic Four: First Steps
note: Director Matt Shakman shot 100% of the film with Arri Alexa 65, LF, and Mini LF cameras, composing every frame for the IMAX ratio — the MCU's sixth production to be fully framed for IMAX from the first shot to the last. Select GT-IMAX venues present sequences in the full 1.43:1 ratio, matching the visual scope of a 70mm IMAX print. The retro-futurist 1960s production design was scaled specifically to fill the taller IMAX canvas throughout.

title: Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice
note: Zack Snyder and DP Larry Fong shot approximately 25 minutes on IMAX MSM 9802 and IMAX MKIII film cameras — the Doomsday battle, the desert "Knightmare" vision, and key confrontation sequences — using Hasselblad and Zeiss 765 prime lenses throughout. Fong and Snyder kept the entire production on photochemical film, making it one of the last major studio blockbusters to shoot IMAX sequences on genuine 15/70mm rather than digital. In IMAX theaters the natively shot sequences expand to the full 1.43:1 ratio, while the anamorphic portions letterbox.

title: Wonder Woman
note: Patty Jenkins and DP Matthew Jensen shot the No Man's Land sequence and the Ares battle with IMAX cameras; the trench-crossing charge was specifically staged to fill the IMAX frame with Diana's shield deflections and her advance across open ground simultaneously from boots to sky. The No Man's Land scene is frequently cited as one of the most effective uses of the IMAX frame in superhero cinema — the 1.90:1 ratio capturing Diana's full-body heroism in a single unbroken composition. It was the first major DC film with a female director to integrate native IMAX capture.

title: Justice League
note: The theatrical version used IMAX cameras for the Themyscira motherbox theft and the Steppenwolf confrontations, with the IMAX footage predominantly sourced from Zack Snyder's pre-reshoots photography. The production's divided authorship contributed to the visual inconsistency noted at the time — the Snyder-originated IMAX sequences have a different photographic character than the Whedon-overseen reshoots. The 2021 "Snyder Cut" was released in a 4:3 format but was not shot with IMAX cameras.

title: Aquaman
note: James Wan and DP Don Burgess shot the underwater kingdom sequences and the Brine King battle with IMAX cameras, using the format's vertical height to convey the full depth and scale of Atlantis — environments where action happens across a vertical axis rather than a horizontal one. The trench sequence — an overwhelming creature attack from every direction — was captured in IMAX to make the surrounding sensation as claustrophobic and vertically disorienting as possible. The film generated $72M in global IMAX box office, validating the format for underwater-set blockbusters.

title: Wonder Woman 1984
note: Patty Jenkins and DP Matthew Jensen used IMAX MSM 9802 film cameras for the Themyscira Amazon Olympics opening sequence and the closing winter coda — both shot on location in the Canary Islands and expanding to the full 1.43:1 IMAX frame — while IMAX-certified digital cameras covered the mall chase and White House action sequences. The film was the first major IMAX theatrical release during the COVID-19 pandemic to also premiere simultaneously on HBO Max. The mixed-format approach gave the mythological bookends a photochemical quality that visually separates them from the film's contemporary Washington D.C. material.

title: The Suicide Squad
note: James Gunn shot the entire film with IMAX-certified cameras — the first DC film he directed fully at the expanded ratio. The Starro the Conqueror finale, with the giant starfish looming over the city, was specifically designed for IMAX's vertical scale, with tentacles and body parts reaching the full height of the frame. Gunn's confidence with the format here directly informed his approach to Guardians Vol. 3 and his full DCU reboot.

title: Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom
note: James Wan deployed IMAX cameras for the Black Manta pursuit sequences and the Black Trident battle, using the expanded ratio to capture the full vertical scale of the underwater environments and Black Manta's aerial combat suit. The film continued the first Aquaman's visual approach, with the taller frame used to emphasize the gap in scale between the human-scale heroes and the enormous marine creatures they fight alongside. It was one of the final DCEU-era films before James Gunn's reboot.

title: Superman
note: James Gunn shot his DCU reboot entirely on IMAX-certified Red Komodo and V-Raptor cameras by DP Henry Braham — the first DCU film shot wholly for IMAX, framing every scene in 1.90:1. The production is notable for its use of Red cameras rather than Arri, demonstrating the expanding range of IMAX-certified hardware now available to filmmakers. Gunn used the full IMAX canvas to give Superman's flight sequences uncompressed vertical sky — the character's defining visual quality.

title: Star Wars: The Force Awakens
note: J.J. Abrams and DP Dan Mindel shot the film primarily on 35mm Kodak film, but used genuine IMAX MKIII Reflex cameras — 15-perf 65mm film cameras, the same format used by Nolan — for the Millennium Falcon chase on Jakku. Abrams told Variety the opportunity to give audiences an action sequence "done in IMAX's natural format was too delicious an idea to pass up," using lenses originally developed by Wally Pfister for The Dark Knight. It was the first Star Wars film in the franchise's 38-year history to include genuine IMAX film photography.

title: Star Wars: The Last Jedi
note: Rian Johnson and DP Steve Yedlin used genuine IMAX 15/70mm film cameras for the Ahch-To island sequences with Luke Skywalker — shot on location in Ireland — alongside ARRI ALEXA 65 for other expanded-ratio material including the Crait salt flat battle and the Holdo hyperspace ramming. The hyperspace ramming is widely considered one of the most visually striking single shots in the franchise's history, delivered in total silence. Johnson's IMAX usage was deliberate and restrained, reserved for moments of maximum emotional and visual weight rather than deployed as a general-action format.

title: Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker
note: Abrams and Mindel used IMAX cameras for the Pasaana speeder chase — shot on a real desert with practical vehicles — and the final Exegol fleet battle, with the Emperor's throne room staged to fill the IMAX frame's full vertical height. The Death Star ruins sequences, shot on location in the Maldives, were captured partly in IMAX with ocean waves crashing against corroded superstructure at the expanded scale. It was the final chapter of the Skywalker Saga to incorporate native IMAX photography.

title: Godzilla vs. Kong
note: Director Adam Wingard and DP Ben Seresin shot the entire film on ARRI ALEXA 65 with IMAX-certified Prime DNA lenses, specifically choosing this camera system to meet IMAX's technical requirements for the largest-scale monster conflict in the franchise. The Hong Kong neon-lit battle was designed to maximize the vertical drama of two titan-scale creatures fighting in an urban canyon, with the ALEXA 65's extraordinary low-light sensitivity capturing the neon environment without artificial augmentation. The film generated $48.5M in global IMAX box office.

title: Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire
note: The first MonsterVerse film to carry the formal "Filmed for IMAX" certification, shot with IMAX MSM cameras and specialized Panavised Canon rigs for the titan sequences — a first for the franchise. Over 45 minutes expand to the exclusive 1.90:1 EAR in IMAX, the most IMAX-expanded content in the MonsterVerse's history. The production designed creature battle sequences specifically around the taller frame to emphasize the monsters' height against Hollow Earth environments and skylines.

title: Star Trek Into Darkness
note: J.J. Abrams and DP Dan Mindel shot approximately 30 minutes on IMAX MSM 9802 film cameras — the Klingon homeworld, the Enterprise-in-freefall, and the climactic San Francisco battle — the same 15/70mm format and Wally Pfister-developed lenses Abrams would later use for The Force Awakens. It was the first Star Trek film to incorporate native IMAX photography, and a nine-minute IMAX preview screened before The Dark Knight Rises drove enormous pre-release interest. The photochemical IMAX sequences give the film a distinct grain and depth that the 35mm anamorphic portions do not share.

title: The Hunger Games: Catching Fire
note: Francis Lawrence and DP Jo Willems shot the final 50 minutes — the entire Quarter Quell arena sequence — on IMAX MSM 9802 film cameras, with three IMAX cameras deployed simultaneously for the most complex shots. The clock-arena, with its rotating sections of death challenges, was designed specifically for IMAX's 1.43:1 ratio, using the full vertical frame to show the scale of each environmental hazard surrounding Katniss at once. It remains one of the most extensive deployments of IMAX film cameras in a non-Nolan production, with half the film's runtime captured natively on 15/70mm.

title: Dune
note: Denis Villeneuve and DP Greig Fraser shot approximately 40% of the film with IMAX-certified Alexa LF and Mini LF cameras, natively composing those sequences for the 1.90:1 ratio — the sandworm approach, the ornithopter arrival, and the spice harvester attack. Villeneuve declared it "a film designed to be seen in IMAX," and Fraser employed a distinctive analog/digital hybrid: digital capture transferred to 35mm print film then rescanned, giving the IMAX photography an unusual photochemical texture never used in a certified IMAX production before. IMAX officially designated it "Filmed for IMAX."

title: Dune: Part Two
note: Villeneuve and Fraser composed the entire sequel for IMAX on ALEXA 65 and Mini LF with fully spherical lenses — a significant expansion from Part One's 40% IMAX coverage to 100%. The Giedi Prime arena sequence was shot in extreme high-contrast black-and-white for the Harkonnen aesthetic, and the Arrakeen attack climax was staged to use the full vertical IMAX canvas at maximum scale. Part Two also received a genuine 15-perf 70mm IMAX print release, placing it alongside Nolan's films in a very small group of digital productions to receive this treatment.

title: Top Gun: Maverick
note: Director Joseph Kosinski and DP Claudio Miranda worked with IMAX to develop custom camera rigs that fit inside operational F/A-18 cockpits — the first time genuine IMAX cameras had been mounted inside military aircraft in flight. The jet sequences were shot with Cruise and the cast physically flying the aircraft, with IMAX cameras a few inches from their faces capturing reactions and the sky beyond at full resolution. The film generated $170M in global IMAX box office, one of the highest-grossing IMAX releases of all time.

title: Avatar: The Way of Water
note: James Cameron shot with IMAX-certified Sony CineAlta Venice cameras in a custom beam-splitter stereoscopic 3D rig — the first IMAX-certified deployment of the Sony Venice in a major 3D production. The underwater sequences required a new submersible lens system co-developed with Sony and Panavision, enabling IMAX 3D capture at operational depths without the distortions of conventional housing systems. Cameron authored the entire film natively in 3D IMAX rather than converting in post, making every frame a genuine stereoscopic IMAX photograph.

title: Joker: Folie à Deux
note: Todd Phillips and DP Lawrence Sher returned to the ARRI ALEXA 65 used on the original Joker for approximately 54 minutes of exclusive 1.90:1 EAR, with the musical sequences specifically choreographed and lit to fill the taller frame with theatrical excess. The film was also released on genuine 15-perf 70mm IMAX prints at 11 venues worldwide — a rare non-Nolan film to receive this treatment, sharing a tier normally occupied only by his productions. The IMAX sequences center on the shared fantasy sequences between Arthur and Harley, using the format's scale as a metaphor for the inflation of Arthur's self-mythology.

title: Alien: Romulus
note: DP Galo Olivares shot on ARRI ALEXA 35 with IMAX certification, using deep-focus photography and claustrophobic framing that deliberately contrasted with the shallow-focus large-format aesthetic dominant in recent blockbusters. The vertical station corridors and ceiling-crawling Alien attack sequences use IMAX's taller frame to make height itself the source of dread — the Alien is always above you, always dropping. It became the highest-grossing horror film in IMAX history at $40M globally.

title: Avatar: Fire and Ash
note: James Cameron shot the third Avatar installment on the same IMAX-certified Sony CineAlta VENICE Rialto stereoscopic 3D rig used for The Way of Water — a custom dual-sensor beam-splitter configuration capturing native 4K 3D, not a post-conversion. Approximately 40% of the film was shot at 48fps High Frame Rate, with Cameron deploying HFR selectively for underwater and action sequences rather than throughout. The IMAX version presents the film in a 1.90:1 open-matte format processed through IMAX's proprietary pipeline, continuing the Avatar series' position as the benchmark for large-format stereoscopic cinema.

title: How to Train Your Dragon
note: The live-action adaptation was shot with Arri Alexa LF and Mini LF IMAX cameras under the "Filmed for IMAX" designation, with the dragon flight and Bewilderbeast sequences designed to use the vertical IMAX frame for the sense of physical height and aerial freedom that the animated films built their identity around. The production used IMAX cameras throughout to integrate creature effects with live-action photography at a consistent, native scale. Key flight and battle sequences expand to the exclusive 1.90:1 ratio in IMAX theaters.

title: Project Hail Mary
note: DP Greig Fraser and director Phil Lord shot the film on the ARRI ALEXA 65 under IMAX's official "Filmed for IMAX" designation, with ARRI Rental engineering a completely custom set of vertical-squeeze anamorphic lenses built specifically for this production — mounted sideways on the ALEXA 65 to natively fill the taller IMAX sensor. The space sequences expand to the full 1.43:1 IMAX ratio, while Earth and memory sequences play in 2.39:1, using the aspect ratio shift as a structural storytelling device in the same vein as Oppenheimer. The custom vertical lens configuration produces distinctive vertical lens flares — an optical signature unique to this film.
